passages.title: The Kite Repair
passages.text:
Omar's kite lay on the grass with a long rip down its middle. The wind had pushed it straight into the branches of the old fig tree, and now the red paper flapped like a broken wing.

"It's ruined," Omar said. He kicked a stone and watched it roll away. The kite festival was only two days away, and he had spent a whole week building that kite.

His grandmother lowered herself onto the bench beside him. She did not say anything at first. Instead, she took a roll of tape and a sheet of tissue paper from her sewing basket. "When I was your age," she said, "my kites broke all the time. The ones I fixed always flew better than the new ones."

Omar frowned. "Why would a broken kite fly better?"

"Because when you fix something, you learn exactly how it works," she answered.

Together they patched the rip, adding a thin strip of bamboo to make the frame stronger. Omar measured the tail again and found it was too short, which explained why the kite had kept spinning. He added three more paper bows.

On the day of the festival, the wind was strong and gusty. Many kites dove toward the ground, but Omar's kite climbed higher and higher, steady as a hawk. Omar looked over at his grandmother and grinned. He knew the patch was the strongest part of all.

passages.title: Nature's Engineers
passages.text:
Beavers are sometimes called nature's engineers because they change the land around them more than almost any other animal except humans.

Building a Dam
A beaver family begins by piling sticks, rocks, and mud across a stream. Because the dam slows the water, a deep, calm pond forms behind it. Beavers patch any leaks quickly, especially when they hear the sound of rushing water.

Why the Pond Matters
The pond protects the beavers. Their lodge, a dome-shaped home of sticks and mud, sits in the middle of the water, and its entrances are underwater. As a result, wolves and other predators cannot easily reach the family inside.

Helping Other Living Things
Beaver ponds also help many other animals. Frogs lay eggs in the still water, ducks find food, and fish hide among the sunken branches. In dry summers, a beaver pond may be the only water for miles, so deer and birds travel to drink there.

Not everyone welcomes beavers. Their dams can flood roads and farmland. However, many scientists now argue that the benefits of beaver ponds are greater than the problems they cause.

passages.title: Our School Needs a Garden
passages.text:
Our school should turn the empty lot behind the library into a vegetable garden. A garden would help students learn, eat better, and work together.

First, a garden is an outdoor classroom. Students could measure plant growth in math, study insects in science, and write observation journals in English. Learning by doing helps facts stick.

Second, students who grow vegetables are more likely to eat them. When children plant a tomato seed, water it, and watch it ripen, they feel proud to taste it. Our cafeteria could even serve the vegetables we grow.

Finally, a garden builds teamwork. Each class could care for its own bed, and older students could help younger ones. Some people say a garden would be too much work. But if every class takes turns, no one group will have to do it all.

The empty lot is wasted space right now. Let's fill it with something that grows—both plants and students.

passages.title: Night Rain
passages.text:
The rain comes tapping on my roof,
A drummer soft and slow;
It hums a song of silver drops
To flowers down below.

The street becomes a shining stream,
The lamps are blurry moons;
The puddles hold the sleeping sky
Like small and quiet spoons.

I pull my blanket to my chin
And listen to the beat;
The rain is singing me to sleep
On soft and silver feet.

passages.title: The Missing Map
passages.text:
CHARACTERS: LAYLA, age 10; KARIM, her younger brother; MS. HASSAN, a park ranger

SCENE: A forest trail at noon. A wooden sign points in two directions.

LAYLA: (turning her backpack upside down) It's gone! The map was right here.
KARIM: (nervously) Maybe we should just go left. Left looks shorter.
LAYLA: Shorter isn't always right. Remember what Dad said? If you're lost, stop and think.
(She sits on a rock and studies the sign. KARIM paces back and forth.)
LAYLA: Look—the sun is high, and the lake was east of the parking lot. The arrow to the right says "Lake Trail."
KARIM: (stopping) So the parking lot is past the lake!
(MS. HASSAN enters from the right, carrying a radio.)
MS. HASSAN: You two look like explorers. Everything all right?
LAYLA: (smiling) We lost our map, but I think we found our way.
MS. HASSAN: Then you found something better than a map—a calm head.

passages.title: The Second Try
passages.text:
I had practiced my speech about sea turtles for two weeks, but when I stood in front of the class, every word I had memorized slipped away like sand through my fingers. My hands shook. I stared at my note cards, and the letters seemed to swim. After three long seconds of silence, I mumbled, "Sorry," and hurried back to my seat.

My best friend, Dana, leaned over. "You know more about turtles than anyone," she whispered. "Just talk like you're telling me." I wanted to believe her, but my face was still burning.

That afternoon, Mr. Farouk asked if I wanted to try again the next day. I almost said no. Then I remembered the baby turtles in the video we had watched—how they crawled toward the ocean even when waves knocked them back again and again.

The next morning, I left my note cards in my desk. I pictured Dana's face in the front row and began with a question: "Did you know that only one in a thousand baby sea turtles survives to adulthood?" Heads lifted. Someone gasped. My voice wobbled at first, but by the end I was smiling, and the class was asking questions I could actually answer.

Walking home, I thought about those turtles again. Being knocked back, I decided, isn't the same as being beaten.

passages.title: Catching Water in the Desert
passages.text:
In some desert villages, rain falls only a few times each year. When it does come, the water rushes over the hard, dry ground and disappears before people can use it. For families who depend on farming, this creates a serious problem: how can they save water when it arrives all at once?

One solution is the rainwater cistern, an underground tank lined with stone or concrete. Gutters on rooftops guide rainwater into pipes that lead to the cistern. Because the tank is underground and covered, the water stays cool and does not evaporate quickly in the heat.

Another solution works on a larger scale. Farmers build low walls of earth called "check dams" across shallow valleys. When a storm comes, the walls slow the water down, giving it time to soak into the soil instead of running away. Over time, the stored moisture allows trees and crops to grow where little grew before.

These methods are not new. Archaeologists have found cisterns that are more than two thousand years old. Today, engineers combine ancient ideas with modern materials, such as plastic liners and solar-powered pumps, to help communities store more water than ever.

passages.title: The Storm: Two Accounts
passages.text:
Account 1 — From Rania's journal, March 12
The wind woke me at 3 a.m. It howled around our building like an angry animal, and something metal kept banging against the balcony. I crawled into my sister's bed, and we counted the seconds between the lightning and the thunder. By morning, our street was a river. Our neighbor's car had water up to its doors. I was scared, but I also felt amazed at how powerful nature can be.

Account 2 — From the Daily Coast News, March 12
A powerful storm struck the coastal district early Thursday morning, bringing winds of up to 90 kilometers per hour and 120 millimeters of rain in six hours. Officials reported flooding on six streets and power outages affecting about 4,000 homes. No injuries were reported. City crews began clearing drains at 7 a.m., and electricity was restored to most homes by noon.

passages.title: City Morning
passages.text:
The city yawns and stretches wide,
Its windows blink awake;
The buses grumble, side by side,
The sidewalks start to shake.

A baker sings a sugared song,
The coffee kettles hiss;
The busy, bustling, buzzing throng
Is rushing—don't you miss

The quiet way the sky turns gold
Above the rooftop line?
Before the day grows loud and bold,
That minute, friend, is mine.

passages.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
passages.text:
The Moon does not make its own light. Instead, it reflects light from the Sun. At every moment, the Sun lights up half of the Moon—the half facing the Sun. What changes from night to night is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth.

As the Moon travels around Earth, our view of the lit half changes. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, so we see almost nothing. This is called a new moon. A few days later, a thin sliver appears, called a crescent. About one week after the new moon, we see half of the Moon's face lit, a phase called the first quarter. After about two weeks, the whole face we see is lit: a full moon. Then the pattern reverses until the next new moon.

The complete cycle takes about 29.5 days. People have used this dependable pattern for thousands of years to create calendars, plan farming, and celebrate holidays.

passages.title: The Last Bus Home
passages.text:
The 6:40 bus was the last one that ran past Yusuf's neighborhood, and he had never missed it. Tonight, though, the robotics club had stayed late to fix a jammed gear, and when Yusuf finally burst through the school doors, the bus was already pulling away, its red taillights shrinking down the hill.

He checked his phone: four percent battery. He typed a quick message to his mother—"Missed bus. Walking."—and watched the screen go black before it sent.

The walk would take forty minutes. Yusuf zipped his jacket and started down the hill, rehearsing what he would say. It wasn't my fault, he practiced. The gear was stuck. Everyone stayed.

Halfway home, he passed Mrs. Qadri's bakery. The lights were still on, and through the window he saw his younger sister, Mariam, sitting at a table with a cup of cocoa. She waved wildly. Mrs. Qadri opened the door. "Your mother called every shop on this street," she said. "Mariam insisted on waiting here because she knew you'd pass by."

Yusuf felt the excuses dissolve. He had spent twenty minutes preparing a defense, and no one had been angry at all—only worried.

Mariam handed him a second cup. "I told Mama you'd walk the bakery way," she said. "You always do."

Yusuf laughed. All this time he had thought of his little sister as someone to look after. He had never considered that she might be looking after him.

passages.title: Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?
passages.text:
More schools are considering a four-day week with longer school days. Supporters believe it would improve learning, but the evidence suggests schools should be cautious.

Supporters argue that a three-day weekend gives students more rest. However, a study of several districts that adopted four-day weeks found that, on average, students' math scores grew more slowly than in similar five-day schools. Longer days also mean that younger students may grow tired by the final hours, when focus is hardest to maintain.

Another claim is that a four-day week saves money. Districts do save some money on buses and heating, but reports show these savings are usually small—often less than two percent of the budget—because teacher salaries, the largest cost, do not change.

Finally, families must find care for children on the fifth day. For working parents, this can be expensive and stressful. Everyone knows that students would rather stay home anyway, so a four-day week would only make them lazier.

A school calendar should be built around what helps students learn most. Until stronger evidence shows that a four-day week improves learning, schools should keep the five-day schedule.

passages.title: Coral Reefs Under Pressure
passages.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet scientists estimate that they support about a quarter of all marine species. Fish shelter in their branches, sea turtles feed on reef plants, and coastlines are protected because reefs break the force of storm waves.

A reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Each polyp lives with microscopic algae inside its tissues. The algae produce food through photosynthesis and share it with the coral; in return, the coral provides the algae with shelter. This partnership also gives coral its brilliant colors.

When ocean water becomes too warm, the partnership breaks down. Stressed corals expel their algae, and without them, the corals turn white—a process called bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If temperatures stay high for weeks, the coral may die.

Scientists are responding in several ways. Some grow young corals in underwater nurseries and transplant them onto damaged reefs. Others search for "heat-tolerant" corals that survive warmer water and breed them. These efforts help, but researchers agree that reefs can only recover on a large scale if ocean temperatures stop rising.

passages.title: Ladder
passages.text:
My grandfather built a ladder
from the branches of a storm-felled tree,
each rung a different width,
each one a year he gave to me.

The first rung, wide and steady,
the year I learned to read;
the third rung, thin and narrow,
the winter I was sick and weak.

I climb it now to reach the apples
that he planted long ago—
each step a story under my feet,
each branch a thing I know.

items.stem: Which sentence best states a theme of “The Kite Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The grandmother says fixed kites fly better, and at the end the patch is “the strongest part of all.” Both details point to this lesson.
explanation.tip: A theme is a lesson about life. Look at what a character learns by the end.

options.label: A
options.text: Fixing something can make it stronger than before.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a fact about one character, not a message about life.

options.label: C
options.text: Kites are hard to fly in strong wind.
options.rationale: This is a detail about wind, not the lesson of the story.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The story never focuses on why festivals are fun.

items.stem: How does Omar feel at the beginning of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar says “It's ruined” and kicks a stone. His words and actions show he is upset.
explanation.tip: Use what a character says and does to figure out feelings.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Kicking a stone shows frustration, not boredom.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Saying “It's ruined” shows he is not calm.

options.label: D
options.rationale: He is proud only at the end, after the kite flies.

items.stem: Which detail best shows that the grandmother is patient and wise?

explanation.whyCorrect: Instead of scolding or rushing, she waits, then teaches Omar through a story. That shows patience and wisdom.
explanation.tip: Character traits are shown through choices, not through objects a character owns.

options.label: A
options.text: The kite festival is in two days.
options.rationale: This detail is about the setting, not the grandmother.

options.label: B
options.text: She lowers herself onto the bench.
options.rationale: This shows how she moves, not what she is like inside.

options.label: C
options.text: She sits quietly, then shares a lesson from her own childhood.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Owning a basket does not show a character trait.

items.stem: From what point of view is “The Kite Repair” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator uses “he,” “she,” and the characters' names, so the story is told in third person.
explanation.tip: First person uses I/me/my. Third person uses he/she/they and names.

options.label: A
options.text: second person — the story speaks to “you”
options.rationale: The story never speaks directly to the reader.

options.label: B
options.text: first person — Omar tells the story using “I”
options.rationale: Omar is called “Omar” and “he,” not “I.”

options.label: C
options.text: first person — the grandmother tells the story
options.rationale: The grandmother is “she”; she is not the narrator.

options.label: D
options.text: third person — a narrator outside the story tells what happens

items.stem: Why did Omar's kite keep spinning before the repair?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story says he “found it was too short, which explained why the kite had kept spinning.”
explanation.tip: Words like “which explained why” point straight to a cause.

options.label: B
options.text: The paper was the wrong color.
options.rationale: Color does not affect how a kite flies, and the story never says so.

options.label: C
options.text: The bamboo frame was too heavy.
options.rationale: The bamboo was added to make it stronger; it was not the problem.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The story says the wind was strong, not gentle.

items.stem: “The red paper flapped like a broken wing.” What does this simile help the reader picture?

explanation.whyCorrect: A simile compares using “like” or “as.” The rip makes the kite flap helplessly, the way a hurt wing would.
explanation.tip: Ask: what two things are being compared, and how are they alike?

options.label: A
options.text: a bird flying high above the tree
options.rationale: The simile describes the torn kite, not a real bird in the sky.

options.label: B
options.text: the torn kite moving weakly, like an injured bird

options.label: C
options.text: the kite flying perfectly at the festival
options.rationale: This happens at the beginning, when the kite is broken.

options.label: D
options.text: a red bird sitting in the fig tree
options.rationale: There is no real bird; the kite is compared to a wing.

items.stem: At the end, the kite climbs “steady as a hawk.” Why did the author choose this comparison?

explanation.whyCorrect: A hawk glides steadily even in wind. The comparison contrasts with the “broken wing” at the start and shows the change.
explanation.tip: Authors often use a second comparison at the end to show how things changed.

options.label: A
options.text: to show the kite is flying away
options.rationale: The kite climbs higher but is still controlled by Omar.

options.label: B
options.text: to warn that hawks might attack kites
options.rationale: Nothing in the story suggests danger from birds.

options.label: C
options.text: to show the repaired kite is now strong and controlled in the wind

options.label: D
options.text: to show the kite is shaped like a bird
options.rationale: The comparison is about how it flies, not its shape.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Kite Repair” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The story moves from the problem, to advice, to the fix, to the result.
explanation.tip: Look for time clues: “at first,” “together,” “on the day of the festival.”

sequence: The kite tears in the fig tree.
Grandmother shares a story about her childhood kites.
Omar finds that the tail is too short.
The kite flies higher than the others at the festival.

items.stem: True or false: Omar's attitude toward broken things changes by the end of the story.

explanation.whyCorrect: At first he says the kite is “ruined.” At the end he knows “the patch was the strongest part of all.”
explanation.tip: Compare a character's thoughts at the beginning and the end to find a change.

items.stem: How many stanzas are in “Night Rain”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A stanza is a group of lines. “Night Rain” has three groups of four lines.
explanation.tip: Stanzas in poems are like paragraphs in stories.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Twelve is the number of lines, not stanzas.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The poem is divided into separate groups of lines.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Count the groups of lines separated by spaces: there are three.

items.stem: Which pair of words from “Night Rain” rhyme?

explanation.whyCorrect: Slow and below both end with the long o sound, so they rhyme.
explanation.tip: Rhyming words have the same ending sound, not just the same letters.

options.label: B
options.rationale: These words do not end with the same sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Stream and moons have different ending sounds.

options.label: D
options.rationale: These end with different sounds.

items.stem: In stanza 1, the rain is called “a drummer soft and slow.” What kind of figurative language is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The poet says the rain IS a drummer without using like or as. That is a metaphor.
explanation.tip: Simile: like/as. Metaphor: says one thing IS another.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A simile uses “like” or “as.” This line does not.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Rhyme is about sounds at line endings, not comparisons.

options.label: D
options.rationale: An idiom is a common saying; this is a fresh comparison.

items.stem: “The puddles hold the sleeping sky.” What does this line mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Puddles act like mirrors at night, so they seem to “hold” the dark, quiet sky.
explanation.tip: Picture the scene. What would you really see in a puddle at night?

options.label: A
options.text: The puddles are deep enough to swim in.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the puddles are deep.

options.label: B
options.text: People are sleeping outside in the rain.
options.rationale: “Sleeping” describes the quiet night sky, not people.

options.label: C
options.text: The puddles reflect the dark night sky.

options.label: D
options.text: The sky has fallen into the street.
options.rationale: The line is figurative; the sky does not actually fall.

items.stem: How does the speaker feel about the rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: The speaker listens under a blanket while the rain “sings” them to sleep—a calm, cozy feeling.
explanation.tip: Notice the describing words a poet chooses; they show the speaker's feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: annoyed because it is too loud
options.rationale: The rain is described as soft and slow.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The speaker pulls a blanket up and falls asleep.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Words like “soft,” “hums,” and “singing me to sleep” are gentle, not scary.

items.stem: In “The Missing Map,” which words are stage directions?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stage directions, usually in parentheses, tell actors what to do or how to move.
explanation.tip: Dialogue = words spoken. Stage directions = actions and feelings in ( ).

options.label: B
options.text: It's gone! The map was right here.
options.rationale: This is dialogue, the words a character says.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This shows who is speaking, not an action.

options.label: D
options.text: SCENE: A forest trail at noon.
options.rationale: This describes the setting, not an action during the play.

items.stem: What is the setting of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: The line “SCENE: A forest trail at noon” tells where and when the play takes place.
explanation.tip: In a play, look for the word SCENE to find the setting.

options.label: A
options.text: a parking lot in the evening
options.rationale: The parking lot is mentioned, but the scene happens on the trail.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Ms. Hassan arrives on the trail; the scene never moves.

options.label: D
options.rationale: They are trying to reach the lake area; they are not there yet.

items.stem: How are Layla and Karim different when they discover the map is missing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Karim says “just go left” nervously, while Layla says “stop and think” and studies the sign.
explanation.tip: Compare what each character says and does in the same moment.

options.label: A
options.text: Both of them panic and start running.
options.rationale: Layla sits on a rock to think.

options.label: B
options.text: Layla wants to give up; Karim makes a plan.
options.rationale: It is Layla who makes the plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Layla stays calm and thinks; Karim wants to rush a choice.

options.label: D
options.text: Karim finds the map; Layla follows him.
options.rationale: The map is never found.

items.stem: Which line from the play best expresses its theme?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ranger sums up the lesson: staying calm and thinking is more useful than any map.
explanation.tip: Characters near the end of a story often say the theme out loud.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a friendly greeting, not the message.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is Karim's quick guess, which the play shows is not wise.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This line starts the problem; it does not state a lesson.

options.label: D
options.text: “Then you found something better than a map—a calm head.”

items.stem: Which TWO details are clues Layla uses to choose the right trail? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Layla uses the sun and what she remembers about the lake's direction to read the sign.
explanation.tip: Text evidence must come from the text AND support the answer.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Layla decides before the ranger arrives.

options.label: B
options.text: The lake was east of the parking lot.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Layla rejects this idea.

items.stem: Why does Layla mention “what Dad said”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Remembering “stop and think” helps her slow down and solve the problem—an inference from her actions afterward.
explanation.tip: An inference = text clues + what you already know.

options.label: A
options.text: She is using advice she learned before to solve a new problem.

options.label: B
options.text: She is blaming Dad for losing the map.
options.rationale: She lost the map; she is not blaming anyone.

options.label: C
options.text: She wants Karim to call their dad.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests calling anyone.

options.label: D
options.text: She is changing the subject to calm down.
options.rationale: The advice is directly connected to their problem.

items.stem: What is the main idea of “Nature's Engineers”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every section explains how beavers change the land and what those changes do.
explanation.tip: The main idea is what the WHOLE text is mostly about. Details support it.

options.label: A
options.text: Beaver dams always cause floods on farms.
options.rationale: The text says dams CAN flood, and scientists see more benefits.

options.label: B
options.text: Beavers build dams and ponds that change the land and help many living things.

options.label: C
options.text: Wolves are the main predators of beavers.
options.rationale: Wolves are one detail in one section.

options.label: D
options.text: Frogs lay their eggs in still water.
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail about other animals.

items.stem: Under which heading would you find out how beaver ponds help ducks?

explanation.whyCorrect: The heading “Helping Other Living Things” introduces frogs, ducks, fish, deer, and birds.
explanation.tip: Headings tell what each section is about. Use them to find information fast.

options.label: A
options.rationale: That section is about protecting the beaver family.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is the title of the whole article.

options.label: D
options.rationale: That section explains how dams are made.

items.stem: According to the article, what is an EFFECT of beavers building a dam?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because the dam slows the water, a deep, calm pond forms.” The pond is the effect.
explanation.tip: Signal words such as because, as a result, and so link causes and effects.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The sound of water makes beavers fix leaks; it is a cause.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is not described as a result of the dam.

options.label: C
options.text: Beavers pile up sticks and mud.
options.rationale: Piling sticks is how they BUILD the dam.

items.stem: Why can't wolves easily reach a beaver family?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says the entrances are underwater, “as a result, wolves … cannot easily reach the family.”
explanation.tip: Find the sentence with “as a result” and read what comes just before it.

options.label: A
options.text: The lodge sits in the pond and its entrances are underwater.

options.label: B
options.text: Wolves are afraid of the sound of water.
options.rationale: This is not in the text.

options.label: C
options.text: The dam is too tall to climb.
options.rationale: The protection comes from the water around the lodge.

options.label: D
options.text: Beavers chase wolves away with sticks.
options.rationale: The article never says this.

items.stem: How is the last paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Not everyone welcomes beavers…However, many scientists…” shows one side, then the other side.
explanation.tip: “However” and “but” often signal a contrasting idea.

options.label: A
options.text: It tells events in the order they happened.
options.rationale: The paragraph weighs two sides; it is not a sequence.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents a problem with beavers and then a counterpoint.

options.label: C
options.text: It describes what a beaver lodge looks like.
options.rationale: The lodge is described earlier.

options.label: D
options.text: It lists the steps for building a dam.
options.rationale: The steps appear in the first section.

items.stem: In the article, what does predators mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence says wolves and other predators try to “reach the family,” so predators are hunters.
explanation.tip: An example word (wolves) can help you define a new word.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Predators are living things that try to reach and catch beavers.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Those are scientists, mentioned separately.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Beavers build homes, but predators are the ones that threaten them.

items.stem: What reason does the author give to support the idea that beavers help other animals?

explanation.whyCorrect: Deer and birds travel to drink at the pond—evidence that beavers help other living things.
explanation.tip: A reason must SUPPORT the point. Check that it matches the point exactly.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a problem, not a benefit to animals.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This describes the lodge.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This explains dam repair, not helping others.

options.label: D
options.text: In dry summers, a beaver pond may be the only water for miles.

items.stem: True or false: The article says that all scientists believe beavers cause more problems than benefits.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says many scientists argue the benefits are GREATER than the problems.
explanation.tip: Watch for absolute words like “all” and “always” in true/false statements.

items.stem: What is the author's opinion in “Our School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence states the claim clearly, and every paragraph supports it.
explanation.tip: In opinion writing, the claim is usually in the first or last sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The school should turn the empty lot into a vegetable garden.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The library is only mentioned as a location.

options.label: C
options.text: Students should eat more vegetables at home.
options.rationale: This is part of one reason, not the main opinion.

options.label: D
options.text: Gardens are too much work for schools.
options.rationale: The author argues against this idea.

items.stem: Which reasons does the author use to support the claim? Choose all that apply.

explanation.whyCorrect: The author uses First, Second, and Finally to introduce three reasons.
explanation.tip: Transition words like First and Finally often introduce reasons.

options.label: A
options.text: A garden is an outdoor classroom.

options.label: B
options.text: A garden will save the school money.
options.rationale: The author never mentions money.

options.label: C
options.text: Students who grow vegetables are more likely to eat them.

items.stem: How does the author respond to people who say a garden is too much work?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author answers the counterclaim: “if every class takes turns, no one group will have to do it all.”
explanation.tip: Strong arguments answer the other side's concerns.

options.label: A
options.text: by saying the cafeteria will do the work
options.rationale: The cafeteria only serves the vegetables.

options.label: B
options.text: by explaining that classes can take turns so no group does it all

options.label: C
options.text: by agreeing that the garden should be small
options.rationale: The author does not agree with the objection.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The author addresses it directly in paragraph 4.

items.stem: In the last sentence, what does “something that grows—both plants and students” suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author plays with two meanings of grow to end with a memorable idea.
explanation.tip: Some words have two meanings at once. Ask what each meaning adds.

options.label: A
options.text: The garden will need more students to work in it.
options.rationale: This misses the double meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Plants grow faster than students do.
options.rationale: No comparison of speed is made.

options.label: C
options.text: Students will learn and develop, just as plants grow.

options.label: D
options.text: Students will become taller by eating vegetables.
options.rationale: “Grow” is used in a figurative sense here.

items.stem: The kitten was timid; it hid under the bed whenever anyone came near. What does timid mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hiding from people is a clue that timid means shy or fearful.
explanation.tip: Read the words after a semicolon; they often explain the word before it.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Hiding shows the opposite of playful.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Nothing mentions food.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Hiding when people come near shows fear, not tiredness.

items.stem: The hikers were exhausted after the long climb, so they rested for an hour. What does exhausted mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: They needed a long rest after a long climb—exhausted means very tired.
explanation.tip: Look at what happens BECAUSE of the word.

options.label: B
options.rationale: No clue is about temperature.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Resting for an hour suggests tiredness.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Nothing says they lost their way.

items.stem: Unlike his cautious sister, who checked the ice twice, Bilal ran straight onto the frozen pond. What does cautious mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Unlike” signals a contrast: Bilal rushed, so his cautious sister must be careful.
explanation.tip: “Unlike,” “but,” and “instead” are contrast clues.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Unlike” shows the sister is the opposite of Bilal, who rushed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Kindness is not discussed.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Checking twice is slow and careful.

items.stem: Which sentence uses bark to mean the outer covering of a tree?

explanation.whyCorrect: Only this sentence describes something you can touch on a tree.
explanation.tip: Multiple-meaning words need the rest of the sentence to choose the meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: The dog's bark woke the baby.
options.rationale: Here bark is the sound a dog makes.

options.label: B
options.text: Don't bark orders at your friends.
options.rationale: Here bark means to speak sharply.

options.label: C
options.text: The bark of the oak felt rough under my hand.

options.label: D
options.text: Did you hear the seal bark?
options.rationale: This is an animal sound.

items.stem: “The pitcher threw the ball so fast that the batter missed it.” What does pitcher mean here?

explanation.whyCorrect: Batter and threw the ball tell you this is a baseball game.
explanation.tip: Look for other words from the same topic (ball, batter).

options.label: A
options.rationale: That is a seller, not a pitcher.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is not a meaning of pitcher.

options.label: C
options.text: a jug used for pouring water
options.rationale: That meaning does not fit a game with a batter.

options.label: D
options.text: a baseball player who throws the ball

items.stem: What does the word reread mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The prefix re- means again, so reread means read again.
explanation.tip: re- = again, un- = not, pre- = before, mis- = wrongly.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Not is the meaning of un- or dis-.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Before is the meaning of pre-.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Wrongly is the meaning of mis-.

items.stem: Match each prefix to its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These four prefixes appear in many Grade 4 words: redo, unkind, preview, misspell.
explanation.tip: Think of a word you know with the prefix, then work out the meaning.

items.stem: What does the word fearless mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -less means without. Fearless = without fear.
explanation.tip: -less = without, -ful = full of.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Full of is the meaning of -ful.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Able to is the meaning of -able.

options.label: D
options.rationale: One who is the meaning of -er.

items.stem: Which word means “able to be broken”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -able means able to be. Breakable = able to be broken.
explanation.tip: Add the suffix to the base word and read the parts in reverse: break + able = able to break.

options.label: A
options.rationale: -er means one who.

options.label: B
options.rationale: re- means again.

options.label: D
options.rationale: -less means without.

items.stem: The Greek root photo means light, and graph means write or draw. What is a photograph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Photo (light) + graph (write/draw) = an image “drawn” by light, the way a camera works.
explanation.tip: Break a long word into roots and combine their meanings.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A bulb does not draw or record.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Phone (sound) is a different root.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Nothing in the roots means night.

items.stem: The Latin root port means carry. Which word means “able to be carried easily”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Port (carry) + -able (able to be) = portable.
explanation.tip: Combine the root's meaning with the suffix's meaning.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A porter is a person who carries things.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Import means to carry INTO a country.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A report carries information back, but it isn't “able to be carried.”

items.stem: Rana said the math test was “a piece of cake.” What did she mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “A piece of cake” is an idiom meaning something is easy.
explanation.tip: Idioms are phrases whose meaning is different from the words themselves.

options.label: A
options.text: She ate cake during the test.
options.rationale: This is the literal meaning, not the idiom.

options.label: C
options.text: The test was hard to finish.
options.rationale: A piece of cake means the opposite.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Idioms do not mean exactly what the words say.

items.stem: What does the adage “Don't count your chickens before they hatch” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: An adage is a well-known saying that gives advice. This one warns against planning on uncertain results.
explanation.tip: Ask: what advice would this saying give a person?

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This misses the lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: Don't depend on something before it actually happens.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The adage is not about real chickens.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a simile?

explanation.whyCorrect: Similes compare two things using like or as: “as soft as a feather.”
explanation.tip: Spot the word like or as connecting two unlike things.

options.label: A
options.text: She spoke softly to the baby.
options.rationale: This is literal.

options.label: B
options.text: Her voice was a gentle breeze.
options.rationale: This is a metaphor; it has no like or as.

options.label: C
options.rationale: No comparison is made.

options.label: D
options.text: Her voice was as soft as a feather.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for enormous?

explanation.whyCorrect: Synonyms have almost the same meaning: enormous and huge both mean very big.
explanation.tip: Synonym = same meaning. Antonym = opposite meaning.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Tiny is an antonym (opposite).

options.label: C
options.rationale: Ancient means very old.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Noisy is about sound, not size.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for generous?

explanation.whyCorrect: A generous person shares; a selfish person does not. They are opposites.
explanation.tip: Test an antonym by putting “not” in front: not generous = selfish.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Giving is a synonym.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Helpful is similar, not opposite.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Kind is close in meaning to generous.

items.stem: Choose the relative pronoun that best completes: “The girl ____ won the race is my cousin.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Who refers to people and connects the clause “won the race” to “the girl.”
explanation.tip: who/whom → people, which → things, that → both.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Use which for things, not people.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Where is a relative adverb for places.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Whose shows ownership.

items.stem: This is the park ____ we had our picnic.

explanation.whyCorrect: Where is a relative adverb that refers to a place (the park).
explanation.tip: where → place, when → time, why → reason.

options.label: A
options.rationale: When refers to a time, not a place.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Who refers to a person.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Why gives a reason.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the PAST progressive tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: Past progressive = was/were + -ing verb. It shows an action that was ongoing in the past.
explanation.tip: Progressive tenses use a form of be + a verb ending in -ing.

options.label: A
options.text: We were walking to school when it started to rain.

options.label: B
options.text: We walk to school every day.
options.rationale: This is the simple present.

options.label: C
options.text: We are walking to school now.
options.rationale: This is the present progressive.

options.label: D
options.text: We will be walking to school tomorrow.
options.rationale: This is the future progressive.

items.stem: Tomorrow at noon, I ____ my grandmother.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow at noon” points to an ongoing action in the future: will be + visiting.
explanation.tip: Time clue words (yesterday, now, tomorrow) tell you which tense to use.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Visited is simple past.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Am visiting is present.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Was shows past time, but “tomorrow” is future.

items.stem: Which modal verb shows that something is REQUIRED? “Visitors ____ wear a helmet in the factory.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Must expresses a rule or requirement.
explanation.tip: Modals: can (ability), may/might (possibility), must (necessity).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Can shows ability or permission.

options.label: B
options.rationale: May shows permission or possibility.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Might shows something is possible, not required.

items.stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?

explanation.whyCorrect: Order: opinion → size → age → shape → color → origin → material → purpose.
explanation.tip: Say it aloud: the correct order usually “sounds right” in English.

options.label: A
options.text: She wore a blue long beautiful dress.
options.rationale: Color should come after opinion and size.

options.label: B
options.text: She wore a beautiful blue long dress.
options.rationale: Size (long) comes before color (blue).

options.label: C
options.text: She wore a long beautiful blue dress.
options.rationale: Opinion (beautiful) comes before size (long).

options.label: D
options.text: She wore a beautiful long blue dress.

items.stem: What is the prepositional phrase in this sentence? “The cat slept under the warm blanket.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition (under) and ends with a noun (blanket).
explanation.tip: Common prepositions: in, on, under, over, near, after, between.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This leaves out the preposition under.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A prepositional phrase starts with the preposition and ends with its object.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

items.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complete sentence has a subject (My brother) and a predicate (plays soccer) and expresses a complete thought.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who or what? Does what? If either is missing, it's a fragment.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone.

options.label: B
options.text: My brother plays soccer on Fridays.

options.label: C
options.rationale: There is no subject—who is running?

options.label: D
options.text: The tall boy with the red hat.
options.rationale: There is no verb telling what the boy does.

items.stem: Which is the best way to fix this run-on? “I finished my homework I went outside to play.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Joining the two sentences with a comma and a conjunction (and) fixes the run-on.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma + and/but/so.

options.label: A
options.text: I finished my homework I went, outside to play.
options.rationale: A comma in the wrong place does not fix the run-on.

options.label: B
options.text: I finished my homework I went outside, to play.
options.rationale: Two sentences are still joined with nothing between them.

options.label: C
options.text: I finished my homework, and then I went outside to play.

options.label: D
options.text: I finished. My homework I went outside to play.
options.rationale: This creates a fragment and an awkward sentence.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ going to the museum on Saturday.”

explanation.whyCorrect: They're is a contraction of they are: They are going to the museum.
explanation.tip: Test it: replace with “they are.” If it works, use they're.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Their shows ownership (their bags).

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is missing the apostrophe.

options.label: C
options.rationale: There tells about a place.

items.stem: Which sentence uses its or it's correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Its (no apostrophe) shows ownership; it's means it is.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes: his, hers, its, ours, theirs.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It's means it is; ownership is its.

options.label: C
options.rationale: It's means it is.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It is raining needs it's.

items.stem: I would like ____ cookies, please.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two is the number 2.
explanation.tip: to = direction, too = also/very, two = 2.

options.label: B
options.rationale: To shows direction or is part of a verb (to go).

options.label: C
options.rationale: Too means also or very.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove “Ali and” to test: “Mom gave the tickets to me.” That sounds correct.
explanation.tip: Cover the other person's name, then choose the pronoun that sounds right.

options.label: A
options.text: Ali and me went to the show.
options.rationale: Subjects need subject pronouns: Ali and I.

options.label: B
options.text: Mom gave the tickets to Ali and me.

options.label: C
options.text: Me and Ali got the tickets.
options.rationale: Me cannot be the subject; use Ali and I.

options.label: D
options.text: Mom gave the tickets to Ali and I.
options.rationale: After a preposition (to), use the object pronoun me.

items.stem: Choose the verb that agrees with the subject: “The students in my class ____ to recess at noon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The subject is students (plural), not class. Plural subjects take go.
explanation.tip: Ignore the prepositional phrase (in my class) to find the real subject.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Is goes with a singular subject.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The subject students is plural, so the verb has no -s.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Has goes with a singular subject.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Sheep is an irregular plural—it stays the same: one sheep, two sheep.
explanation.tip: Irregular plurals don't add -s: child → children, mouse → mice, sheep → sheep.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Swim is irregular: swim → swam → swum.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs change their spelling in the past tense instead of adding -ed.

items.stem: Which sentence compares correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare TWO things with -er (or more); compare THREE or more with -est (or most).
explanation.tip: Never use more AND -er together.

options.label: A
options.text: This puzzle is more harder than the last one.
options.rationale: Do not use more with -er.

options.label: B
options.text: This puzzle is hardest than the last one.
options.rationale: Use -est for three or more things, and never with than.

options.label: C
options.text: This puzzle is most hard than the last one.
options.rationale: Most is for three or more things.

options.label: D
options.text: This puzzle is harder than the last one.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids a double negative?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use only one negative word in a sentence: don't + any.
explanation.tip: Negative words: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, none.

options.label: A
options.text: I don't have any homework tonight.

options.label: B
options.text: I haven't got no homework tonight.
options.rationale: Haven't and no are two negatives.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Don't and never are two negatives.

options.label: D
options.text: I don't have no homework tonight.
options.rationale: Don't and no are two negatives.

items.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, months, and names of places.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns (specific names) need capitals.

options.label: A
options.text: Last July, my Family visited Riyadh.
options.rationale: Family is a common noun here.

options.label: B
options.text: Last July, my family visited Riyadh.

options.label: C
options.text: last July, My family visited Riyadh.
options.rationale: Capitalize the first word; don't capitalize my in the middle.

options.label: D
options.text: Last july, my family visited riyadh.
options.rationale: Months and city names are proper nouns.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Put quotation marks around the exact words spoken, with the question mark inside.
explanation.tip: Punctuation of the spoken words stays inside the quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: “Can we go to the park,” asked Huda?
options.rationale: The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.text: Can we go to the park? “asked Huda.”
options.rationale: Only the spoken words go inside quotation marks.

options.label: C
options.text: “Can we go to the park?” asked Huda.

options.label: D
options.text: “Can we go to the park”? asked Huda.
options.rationale: End punctuation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

items.stem: Where does the comma belong? “I wanted to play outside but it was raining.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so) that joins two complete sentences.
explanation.tip: Remember FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The comma comes before but, not after.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Two complete sentences joined by but need a comma.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The comma goes before the conjunction that joins two sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: after outside: “I wanted to play outside, but it was raining.”

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Beauty + ful: change y to i and add -ful = beautiful.
explanation.tip: When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i before adding most suffixes.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Missing the u after the e-a.

options.label: C
options.rationale: When adding -ful, change y to i.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Missing the a.

items.stem: Add -ing to the word hop: I am ____ on one foot.

explanation.whyCorrect: Hop has one short vowel and ends in one consonant, so double the p: hopping.
explanation.tip: Short vowel + one consonant → double it before -ing or -ed.

items.stem: Which word is the most precise replacement for went in: “The rabbit went across the yard when it heard the dog”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Darted shows a quick, sudden movement—exactly what a frightened rabbit does.
explanation.tip: Replace vague verbs (went, got, said) with words that show HOW.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Moved is just as vague as went.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Walked doesn't show the rabbit's fear or speed.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Was is not an action.

items.stem: Which sentence would be best in a formal report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Formal language is clear and serious, without slang or casual words.
explanation.tip: Ask: would this sound right in a science textbook?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Formal writing uses full sentences, not shortcuts.

options.label: B
options.text: So, like, the sunny plants won.
options.rationale: Like and won are casual words.

options.label: C
options.text: The experiment showed that plants grew taller in sunlight.

options.label: D
options.text: The plants totally grew way taller in the sun!
options.rationale: Totally and way are informal.

items.stem: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about why owls are good night hunters?

explanation.whyCorrect: A topic sentence tells the main idea the whole paragraph will explain.
explanation.tip: A good topic sentence is broad enough to cover all the details.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Too general—it doesn't introduce the topic of night hunting.

options.label: B
options.text: I saw an owl once at my uncle's farm.
options.rationale: This is a personal story, not a topic sentence for this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a detail, not the main point.

options.label: D
options.text: Owls have special features that make them excellent hunters at night.

items.stem: Choose the best linking word: “Bats sleep during the day. ____, they hunt for insects at night.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences contrast day and night, so a contrast transition fits.
explanation.tip: Transitions show how ideas connect: adding, contrasting, giving examples, or showing time.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Because cannot start this kind of contrast.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Also adds a similar idea; this idea contrasts.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the first.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to make a clear story.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences follow time order: waking, getting ready, a problem, and the solution.
explanation.tip: Use time words (first, when, later) to help readers follow events.

sequence: Sami woke up early on the first day of school.
He packed his bag and ate breakfast quickly.
When he reached the gate, he realized he had forgotten his lunch.
Luckily, his father arrived a minute later holding the lunch box.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the opinion “Students should have longer lunch breaks”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A strong reason connects directly to the opinion and can be supported with facts.
explanation.tip: Ask: does this detail prove WHY the opinion is right?

options.label: A
options.text: Lunch is my favorite part of the day.
options.rationale: This is a personal feeling, not a reason others can check.

options.label: B
options.text: Many students do not have time to finish their food in 20 minutes.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This fact doesn't support longer breaks.

options.label: D
options.rationale: School start time is not about lunch length.

items.stem: From whose point of view is “The Second Try” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator says “I” and describes their own shaking hands and burning face.
explanation.tip: First-person narrators use I, me, and my and are part of the story.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Dana is a character the narrator talks about.

options.label: B
options.text: an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts
options.rationale: The story uses “I” and only shares one person's thoughts.

options.label: C
options.text: the student giving the speech, in first person

options.label: D
options.rationale: Mr. Farouk is described from the outside.

items.stem: How does the first-person point of view affect how the first speech is described?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the narrator tells their own experience, we get feelings and sensations, not just events.
explanation.tip: Ask: what can THIS narrator know and feel? How does that shape what we learn?

options.label: A
options.text: Readers learn exactly what every classmate was thinking.
options.rationale: A first-person narrator cannot know others' thoughts.

options.label: B
options.text: Readers see the speech mainly through Dana's eyes.
options.rationale: Dana does not narrate.

options.label: C
options.text: Readers get a calm, factual report of the speech.
options.rationale: The description is emotional, not factual.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers feel the narrator's panic from the inside, like the words “slipped away like sand.”

items.stem: Which sentence best states the theme of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last line—“Being knocked back … isn't the same as being beaten”—expresses the theme.
explanation.tip: Theme often appears in what a character realizes at the end.

options.label: A
options.text: A setback is not a failure if you keep trying.

options.label: B
options.text: Sea turtles have a hard life in the ocean.
options.rationale: This is a topic of the speech, not the story's lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers should give students second chances.
options.rationale: This focuses on the teacher, not the narrator's growth.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The narrator leaves the cards behind, but that is a detail, not the theme.

items.stem: How does the memory of the baby turtles help the narrator?

explanation.whyCorrect: The turtles keep crawling despite waves, and the narrator applies that lesson to their own situation.
explanation.tip: When a character remembers something, ask how it changes their next action.

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the narrator decide to skip the speech.
options.rationale: The narrator decides to try again.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives the narrator courage to try the speech again.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the narrator want a new speech topic.
options.rationale: The narrator keeps the same topic.

options.label: D
options.text: It reminds the narrator to study more facts.
options.rationale: The narrator already knows the facts well.

items.stem: “Every word I had memorized slipped away like sand through my fingers.” What does this simile show?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sand runs out of your hand even when you grip it—just as the words escaped the nervous narrator.
explanation.tip: Figure out what quality the two things share.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The rest of the paragraph shows fear.

options.label: B
options.text: The words were written in the sand.
options.rationale: The comparison is about memory, not writing.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator could not hold on to the words, no matter how hard they tried.

options.label: D
options.text: The narrator was standing on a beach.
options.rationale: The speech is in a classroom; the sand is figurative.

items.stem: Compare the narrator at the first speech with the narrator at the second speech.

explanation.whyCorrect: The change from shaking and mumbling to smiling and answering questions shows growth.
explanation.tip: Compare the same character at two points in a story to see how they change.

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator reads more cards the second time.
options.rationale: The cards stay in the desk the second time.

options.label: B
options.text: The narrator is nervous both times and never improves.
options.rationale: By the end, the narrator is smiling and answering questions.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator is confident both times.
options.rationale: The narrator's hands shook the first time.

options.label: D
options.text: First the narrator relies on note cards and freezes; second the narrator speaks freely and engages the class.

items.stem: Which TWO quotations show that the second speech went well?

explanation.whyCorrect: The class reacting with interest and asking questions shows success.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that directly proves the answer, not details that point the other way.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This happens before the second speech.

options.label: C
options.text: “the class was asking questions I could actually answer.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: This shows some nervousness.

items.stem: True or false: The narrator starts the second speech with a surprising fact to grab the audience's attention.

explanation.whyCorrect: Starting with “Did you know…?” and a surprising statistic makes heads lift—an attention-grabbing hook.
explanation.tip: Infer the purpose of a choice by looking at its effect on others.

items.stem: How do the three stanzas of “City Morning” fit together?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first two stanzas build noise and activity; the last stanza contrasts it with a quiet golden sky.
explanation.tip: Look for a turn: a word like “but” or a change in mood between stanzas.

options.label: A
options.text: Stanzas 1–2 show the city waking up loudly; stanza 3 turns to the speaker's quiet moment.

options.label: B
options.text: The stanzas tell events from evening to midnight.
options.rationale: The poem takes place in the morning.

options.label: C
options.text: Every stanza repeats the same idea in the same way.
options.rationale: The last stanza shifts to a new idea.

options.label: D
options.text: Each stanza describes a different city.
options.rationale: All three describe the same morning.

items.stem: “The city yawns and stretches wide.” What kind of figurative language is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The city is given human actions (yawning and stretching), so this is personification.
explanation.tip: Personification = giving human qualities to something that isn't human.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Yawn is not a sound word here.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Rhyme is about sounds, not giving human actions.

options.label: D
options.rationale: There is no like or as.

items.stem: “The busy, bustling, buzzing throng.” Which sound device is used?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeating the starting sound b in nearby words is alliteration. It makes the line sound fast and noisy.
explanation.tip: Alliteration = same first consonant sound in a row of words.

options.label: A
options.text: onomatopoeia — every word is a sound
options.rationale: Busy and bustling are not sound words.

options.label: B
options.rationale: No full line repeats.

options.label: D
options.text: rhyme — the words end with the same sound
options.rationale: The words share beginning sounds, not ending sounds.

items.stem: How does the speaker reflect on the morning in the last stanza?

explanation.whyCorrect: “That minute, friend, is mine” shows the speaker treasures the calm moment.
explanation.tip: In poems, the speaker's final lines often reveal their feelings about the topic.

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker wishes the city were louder.
options.rationale: The speaker prefers the quiet minute.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker complains about the baker's singing.
options.rationale: The baker is part of the description, not a complaint.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker plans to leave the city forever.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests leaving.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker values a short, quiet moment before the busy day begins.

items.stem: What problem does “Catching Water in the Desert” describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 1 explains that rare rain rushes over dry ground and disappears.
explanation.tip: Problem-and-solution texts usually state the problem first.

options.label: A
options.text: Rainwater rushes away before people can use it.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Cost is not discussed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The text never says this.

options.label: D
options.text: Cisterns are too old to work.
options.rationale: Old cisterns are evidence that the idea works.

items.stem: Which solutions does the article describe? Choose all that apply.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains two solutions: cisterns and check dams.
explanation.tip: Look for signal words: One solution…, Another solution….

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is not mentioned.

items.stem: Why does water in a cistern evaporate slowly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because the tank is underground and covered, the water stays cool and does not evaporate quickly.”
explanation.tip: Because introduces a cause.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Check dams are a separate solution.

options.label: B
options.text: The tank is underground and covered, so it stays cool.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Gutters only guide water into pipes.

options.label: D
options.text: Plastic liners stop water from moving.
options.rationale: Liners are a modern material; the article links slow evaporation to being underground and covered.

items.stem: Which TWO main ideas does the article develop?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains the problem and then shows old and new ways to store water.
explanation.tip: Grade 5 texts may have more than one main idea. Check each section.

options.label: A
options.text: Deserts are hot, and rain is dangerous.
options.rationale: Rain is helpful when it can be saved.

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers dislike storms, and walls stop floods.
options.rationale: The walls help water soak in; they don't just stop floods.

options.label: C
options.text: Desert communities face a water problem, and both ancient and modern methods help solve it.

options.label: D
options.text: Archaeologists study old tanks, and engineers build pumps.
options.rationale: These are supporting details.

items.stem: “The water stays cool and does not evaporate quickly in the heat.” What does evaporate mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Heat causes water to disappear into the air—a cause/effect clue to the meaning.
explanation.tip: L.5.4: cause-and-effect relationships can reveal meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Flowing is not caused by heat.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Nothing suggests dirt.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Freezing happens in cold, not heat.

options.label: D
options.text: turn into vapor and disappear into the air

items.stem: Why does the author mention that some cisterns are more than two thousand years old?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence before says “These methods are not new.” The ancient cisterns are evidence for that point.
explanation.tip: Find which point a detail supports by reading the sentence just before it.

options.label: A
options.text: to support the point that these water-saving methods are not new

options.label: B
options.text: to show that cisterns break easily
options.rationale: Surviving 2,000 years suggests the opposite.

options.label: C
options.text: to explain how solar pumps work
options.rationale: Pumps are mentioned later as modern.

options.label: D
options.text: to prove deserts used to have more rain
options.rationale: The detail is about the method, not the climate.

items.stem: How are the two accounts of the storm different?

explanation.whyCorrect: A firsthand account tells personal experience; a secondhand account reports facts.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who wrote it? Were they there? What do they focus on?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Both describe the same March 12 storm.

options.label: B
options.text: Rania's journal describes feelings and experiences; the news report gives facts and numbers.

options.label: C
options.text: The news report describes being scared at night.
options.rationale: Feelings appear only in the journal.

options.label: D
options.text: Both accounts give exact wind speeds.
options.rationale: Only the news report gives wind speed.

items.stem: Which information appears ONLY in the news report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Only the reporter gives details about crews and power being restored.
explanation.tip: Compare point of view: what can each writer know?

options.label: A
options.text: The storm happened during the night.
options.rationale: Both accounts show it happened early in the morning.

options.label: B
options.text: There was flooding on the streets.
options.rationale: Both mention flooding.

options.label: C
options.text: Electricity was restored to most homes by noon.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Both describe strong wind.

items.stem: In Rania's journal, the wind “howled … like an angry animal.” This is an example of —

explanation.whyCorrect: The wind is compared to an animal using like, so it is a simile.
explanation.tip: Simile = like/as.

options.label: A
options.rationale: It is a new comparison, not a common saying.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It is a figurative description.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The comparison uses like.

items.stem: About one week after a new moon, what phase do we see?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says about one week after the new moon we see the first quarter.
explanation.tip: In sequence texts, notice time words: a few days later, about one week, after two weeks.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is the starting point.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A full moon appears after about two weeks.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A crescent appears just a few days after the new moon.

items.stem: Put the Moon's phases in order, starting with the new moon.

explanation.whyCorrect: The lit part we can see grows from nothing, to a sliver, to half, to the whole face.
explanation.tip: Use the time clues in the text to order events.

sequence: new moon
crescent
first quarter
full moon

items.stem: Why do we see almost nothing during a new moon?

explanation.whyCorrect: The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so its lit half faces away from us.
explanation.tip: Read carefully for the scientific reason, not a guess from everyday experience.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The Sun always lights half the Moon.

options.label: B
options.text: The lit side of the Moon is facing away from Earth.

options.label: C
options.text: Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon.
options.rationale: The text explains phases by viewing angle, not Earth's shadow.

options.label: D
options.text: Clouds always cover the Moon at that time.
options.rationale: Weather is not mentioned.

items.stem: True or false: According to the article, the amount of the Moon that the Sun lights up changes every night.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Sun always lights half the Moon. What changes is how much of that lit half WE can see.
explanation.tip: Watch for statements that sound right but change one key detail.

items.stem: “People have used this dependable pattern for thousands of years.” What does dependable mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: A pattern used for calendars must be reliable; depend + -able = able to be depended on.
explanation.tip: Combine context with word parts to check your answer.

options.label: A
options.rationale: People could use it for calendars, so it must be easy to predict.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It has been used for thousands of years.

options.label: C
options.text: able to be trusted to happen the same way

options.label: D
options.rationale: Brightness is not related to the word.

items.stem: The Greek root tele means far, and scope means look. What is a telescope?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tele (far) + scope (look) = a tool to look at far objects.
explanation.tip: Learn common roots: tele, scope, graph, phon, auto, bio.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Tele means far, not close.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Graph means write.

options.label: C
options.text: a tool for hearing far away
options.rationale: Phone means sound; scope means look.

options.label: D
options.text: a tool for looking at things far away

items.stem: Match each root to its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Audience (hear), visible (see), transport (carry), construct (build).
explanation.tip: Think of a word you know with the root to remember its meaning.

items.stem: The Latin root dict means say or speak. Which word means “to say what will happen in the future”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pre (before) + dict (say) = to say beforehand.
explanation.tip: Combine the prefix and the root meanings.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A dictionary contains words but doesn't describe the future.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Dictate means to say aloud for someone to write.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Contra (against) + dict = to say the opposite.

items.stem: In which sentence does wind mean to turn or twist?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wind (rhymes with find) is a verb meaning to turn. Wind (rhymes with pinned) is moving air.
explanation.tip: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings and sometimes different pronunciations.

options.label: A
options.text: The wind felt cold this morning.
options.rationale: This is moving air.

options.label: B
options.text: Please wind the string around the spool.

options.label: C
options.text: The wind blew the leaves away.
options.rationale: Here wind is moving air.

options.label: D
options.text: A strong wind knocked the sign over.
options.rationale: This is moving air.

items.stem: “The doctor wound a bandage around the wound.” What do the two words mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wound (rhymes with sound) is the past of wind; wound (rhymes with moon) is an injury.
explanation.tip: Use each word's job in the sentence (action or thing) to choose its meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The order is reversed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The second wound is a thing that is wrapped.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The first wound is an action.

items.stem: What does the proverb “Actions speak louder than words” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: This proverb teaches that behavior proves what a person really means.
explanation.tip: Proverbs give advice or a truth about life.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The proverb is not about quiet people.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: C
options.text: Words are more important than actions.
options.rationale: It means the opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: What people do shows more than what they say.

items.stem: “We're in the same boat,” said Lina when both of them forgot their homework. What does she mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “In the same boat” means facing the same problem.
explanation.tip: Idioms can't be understood word by word.

options.label: A
options.text: They are in the same situation.

options.label: B
options.rationale: There is no real boat.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the literal meaning.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The idiom is about sharing a situation, not rowing.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a metaphor?

explanation.whyCorrect: The metaphor says the classroom IS a beehive to show how busy it was.
explanation.tip: Metaphors compare without like or as.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is literal.

options.label: B
options.text: The classroom was a beehive of activity.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a literal fact.

options.label: D
options.text: The classroom was as busy as a beehive.
options.rationale: This uses as … as, so it is a simile.

items.stem: Which pair of words are antonyms?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ancient means very old; modern means new—opposites.
explanation.tip: Antonyms are opposites.

options.label: A
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

options.label: B
options.rationale: These are similar.

options.label: D
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

items.stem: Compared to the noisy cafeteria, the library felt serene. What does serene mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comparison with noisy shows that serene means quiet and calm.
explanation.tip: L.5.4.a: comparisons in a sentence are clues to meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The comparison with noisy suggests the opposite.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Nothing mentions light.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Serene describes a peaceful feeling, not interest.

items.stem: Which resource would BEST help you find a synonym for happy?

explanation.whyCorrect: A thesaurus lists synonyms and antonyms.
explanation.tip: Dictionary → meaning and pronunciation; thesaurus → synonyms.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A calendar shows dates.

options.label: C
options.rationale: An encyclopedia gives facts about topics.

options.label: D
options.rationale: An atlas contains maps.

items.stem: Which word is a conjunction in this sentence? “I wanted pizza, but my sister wanted pasta.”

explanation.whyCorrect: But joins two ideas, so it is a conjunction.
explanation.tip: Coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Pasta is a noun.

options.label: C
options.rationale: My is a possessive pronoun.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Wanted is a verb.

items.stem: Which word is an interjection? “Wow, that roller coaster was fast!”

explanation.whyCorrect: An interjection is a word that shows strong feeling, often followed by a comma or exclamation point.
explanation.tip: Interjections: wow, oh, ouch, hooray.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Was is a verb.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is a demonstrative.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Fast is an adjective.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect tense?
