explanation.whyCorrect: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
explanation.tip: Perfect tenses use has, have, had, or will have.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is past perfect.

options.label: B
options.text: She will have finished by Friday.
options.rationale: This is future perfect.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is simple past.

options.label: D
options.text: She has finished her science project.

items.stem: By the time we arrived, the movie ____ already started.

explanation.whyCorrect: Past perfect (had + participle) shows an action finished before another past action.
explanation.tip: Two past actions? The earlier one often uses had.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Have does not match the singular movie or past time.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Has is present perfect; the sentence is about the past.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Will have is future.

items.stem: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in verb tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yesterday shows past time, so walk should be walked to match bought.
explanation.tip: Keep verb tenses consistent unless the time actually changes.

options.label: A
options.text: Every day we walk to the store and buy milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs are in the present.

options.label: B
options.text: Yesterday we walk to the store and bought milk.

options.label: C
options.text: Tomorrow we will walk to the store and buy milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs refer to the future.

options.label: D
options.text: Yesterday we walked to the store and bought milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs are in the past.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Last summer” and “stayed” show past time, so the verb must be traveled.
explanation.tip: Find the time clue, then check every verb against it.

items.stem: Which pair of correlative conjunctions completes the sentence? “You can ____ walk ____ ride your bike.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.
explanation.tip: Memorize the four pairs.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Both pairs with and.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Not only pairs with but also.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Neither pairs with nor.

items.stem: Neither my brother ____ my sister likes spinach.

explanation.whyCorrect: Neither always pairs with nor.
explanation.tip: N goes with N: Neither → Nor.

options.label: A
options.rationale: But is not part of this pair.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Or pairs with either.

options.label: C
options.rationale: And pairs with both.

items.stem: Which sentence has correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each is singular, so the pronoun and noun that follow must be singular.
explanation.tip: Words like each, every, and everyone are singular.

options.label: A
options.text: Each student brought his or her own lunch.

options.label: B
options.text: Each student brought their own lunches.
options.rationale: Each is singular, so lunches should be lunch.

options.label: C
options.text: Each student brought our own lunch.
options.rationale: Our does not refer to student.

options.label: D
options.text: Each student brought its own lunch.
options.rationale: Its is for things, not people.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a relative adverb correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: When refers to a time (day).
explanation.tip: where → place, when → time, why → reason.

options.label: A
options.text: This is the reason when I'm late.
options.rationale: Reason needs why.

options.label: B
options.text: I remember the day when we moved here.

options.label: C
options.text: That's the house why I grew up.
options.rationale: House is a place, so use where.

options.label: D
options.text: I remember the day where we moved here.
options.rationale: Day is a time, so use when.

items.stem: Which sentence is complex (has an independent clause and a dependent clause)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Although it was late” cannot stand alone, so the sentence is complex.
explanation.tip: Dependent clauses often begin with although, because, when, if, since.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is one independent clause.

options.label: C
options.text: Although it was late, we finished the game.

options.label: D
options.text: It was late, and we finished the game.
options.rationale: This is compound: two independent clauses.

items.stem: Which word correctly completes: “This is the ____ book I have ever read.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing with all books ever read needs the superlative best.
explanation.tip: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Good is irregular; goodest is not a word.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Use best, not more good.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Better compares two things.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use commas to separate three or more items in a series.
explanation.tip: Put a comma after each item except the last.

options.label: A
options.text: We packed sandwiches, apples, and juice.

options.label: B
options.text: We packed, sandwiches, apples, and juice.
options.rationale: No comma after the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: We packed sandwiches apples, and juice.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after sandwiches.

options.label: D
options.text: We packed sandwiches, apples, and, juice.
options.rationale: No comma after and.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory element?

explanation.whyCorrect: Put a comma after an introductory phrase or clause.
explanation.tip: Read it aloud; the comma goes where you naturally pause after the opener.

options.label: A
options.text: After the bell rang the students, lined up.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: After the bell rang, the students lined up.

options.label: C
options.text: After, the bell rang the students lined up.
options.rationale: After is part of the introductory phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: After the bell, rang the students lined up.
options.rationale: The comma splits the clause.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma for direct address?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma to set off the name of the person you are speaking to.
explanation.tip: Direct address = talking TO someone by name.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the name.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The comma should come right after the name.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a tag question?

explanation.whyCorrect: Separate a tag question from the rest of the sentence with a comma.
explanation.tip: Tag questions: isn't it? didn't you? won't they?

options.label: A
options.text: You finished, the report didn't you?
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: You finished the report, didn't you.
options.rationale: A question needs a question mark.

options.label: C
options.text: You finished the report didn't you?
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the tag.

options.label: D
options.text: You finished the report, didn't you?

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to write the title of a book?

explanation.whyCorrect: Book titles are italicized (or underlined when handwritten).
explanation.tip: Long works (books, movies) → italics; short works (poems, songs) → quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: My favorite book is Charlotte's Web.

options.label: B
options.text: My favorite book is charlotte's web.
options.rationale: Titles need capital letters.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Quotation marks are for short works such as stories and poems.

options.label: D
options.text: My favorite book is CHARLOTTE'S WEB.
options.rationale: Do not write titles in all capitals.

items.stem: Change to plural: one shelf, two ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: For many words ending in f, change f to v and add -es: shelf → shelves.
explanation.tip: f/fe → ves: leaf → leaves, knife → knives.

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Necessary has one c and two s's.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: one Collar and two Sleeves.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Only one c.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Two s's are needed.

options.label: D
options.rationale: One c and two s's.

items.stem: Which sentence best combines these? “The fox was hungry. The fox searched the field.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Moving hungry before fox combines the ideas into one clear sentence.
explanation.tip: Combine by turning a short sentence into an adjective or phrase.

options.label: A
options.text: The fox was hungry, the fox searched the field.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice that repeats the fox.

options.label: B
options.text: The fox was hungry and the fox searched.
options.rationale: This repeats the subject and drops a detail.

options.label: C
options.text: The hungry fox searched the field.

options.label: D
options.text: Hungry. The fox searched the field.
options.rationale: This creates a fragment.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: “Recycling saves resources. ____, it reduces the amount of trash in landfills.”

explanation.whyCorrect: In addition adds another supporting point.
explanation.tip: Transitions: adding (also, in addition), contrast (however), example (for instance), result (as a result).

options.label: A
options.rationale: The second idea is another benefit, not a result.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the first.

options.label: C
options.rationale: However shows a contrast; these ideas agree.

items.stem: Which phrase BEST links a reason to the opinion in an essay?

explanation.whyCorrect: Linking phrases such as “this matters because” or “consequently” connect reasons to opinions.
explanation.tip: W.5.1.c: link opinion and reasons with words, phrases, and clauses.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This begins a story, not an argument.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a place, not a link.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This ends a story.

items.stem: Put the sentences in order to show a clear sequence in a narrative.

explanation.whyCorrect: Transitions (At first, Then, Moments later, Finally) show the order of events.
explanation.tip: W.5.3.c: use transitional words to manage the sequence of events.

sequence: At first, the cave seemed silent and empty.
Then a faint drip echoed from the darkness.
Moments later, my flashlight caught the glitter of an underground pool.
Finally, I understood where the sound had been coming from.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most concrete and sensory details?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stung, sprinted, and slippery help readers feel and see the moment.
explanation.tip: Show, don't tell: use verbs and details the reader can sense.

options.label: A
options.text: It was raining a lot outside.
options.rationale: This tells, but doesn't show.

options.label: B
options.text: The cold rain stung my cheeks as I sprinted across the slippery bridge.

options.label: C
options.text: I didn't like the rain that day.
options.rationale: This states a feeling without details.

options.label: D
options.text: The weather was bad as I went across.
options.rationale: Bad and went are vague.

items.stem: Which is the best way to take notes from a source without plagiarizing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paraphrasing and listing sources shows respect for others' work.
explanation.tip: Read, cover the text, and write what you remember in your own words.

options.label: A
options.text: Change one word in each sentence.
options.rationale: Small changes are still copying.

options.label: B
options.rationale: You must list sources you use.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the key facts in your own words and record the source.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Copying is plagiarism unless you quote and credit the source.

items.stem: What event sets the plot of “The Last Bus Home” in motion?

explanation.whyCorrect: Missing the 6:40 bus creates the problem that drives the rest of the story.
explanation.tip: The inciting incident is the first event that creates the story's problem.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This makes the problem worse, but it isn't the first event.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This happens later, as part of the resolution.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This happens near the end.

options.label: D
options.text: Yusuf misses the last bus after robotics club runs late.

items.stem: How does Yusuf respond to his problem during the walk home?

explanation.whyCorrect: The italic lines (“It wasn't my fault…”) show him preparing to defend himself.
explanation.tip: RL.6.3: notice how characters respond as the plot moves forward.

options.label: A
options.text: He rehearses excuses because he expects to be blamed.

options.label: B
options.text: He runs to catch the bus at the next stop.
options.rationale: He decides to walk the whole way.

options.label: C
options.text: He forgets about the problem completely.
options.rationale: He spends twenty minutes preparing a defense.

options.label: D
options.text: He calls his mother every few minutes.
options.rationale: His phone is dead.

items.stem: How does Yusuf change by the end of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph states his new understanding about Mariam.
explanation.tip: Character change is often revealed in the final thoughts of the main character.

options.label: A
options.text: He becomes angry at his mother for worrying.
options.rationale: He laughs and feels relieved.

options.label: B
options.text: He realizes his younger sister cares for him, not just the other way around.

options.label: C
options.text: He learns to always charge his phone.
options.rationale: This lesson is never stated.

options.label: D
options.text: He decides to quit the robotics club.
options.rationale: The club is never mentioned again.

items.stem: The story is told in third person but follows only Yusuf's thoughts. How does this affect the reader?

explanation.whyCorrect: A limited narrator lets readers discover the truth at the same moment as the character.
explanation.tip: RL.6.6: ask how the narrator's point of view develops the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers learn about every character equally.
options.rationale: The narration stays close to Yusuf.

options.label: B
options.text: Readers know from the start that his family is not angry.
options.rationale: We only learn this when Yusuf does.

options.label: C
options.text: Readers share Yusuf's worry, so they are surprised along with him that no one is angry.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers understand Mariam's thoughts during the whole story.
options.rationale: We don't hear Mariam's thoughts.

items.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yusuf prepares a defense, but discovers his family was only worried. That realization is the theme.
explanation.tip: A theme is a universal statement, not a summary of the plot.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a detail, not a universal message.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is practical advice, not the theme.

options.label: C
options.text: Bakeries are good places to wait.
options.rationale: This is about the setting.

options.label: D
options.text: People who care about us may be worried rather than angry when things go wrong.

items.stem: “Yusuf felt the excuses dissolve.” What does the word dissolve suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Like sugar in water, the excuses vanish once he sees no one is angry.
explanation.tip: When a word is used figuratively, think about its literal meaning first, then apply it.

options.label: A
options.text: His prepared excuses disappeared because they were no longer needed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: He talks and laughs afterward.

options.label: C
options.text: He wrote his excuses on paper.
options.rationale: The excuses were only in his mind.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Dissolve is figurative here.

items.stem: Which TWO details best support the idea that Mariam knows her brother well?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mariam predicted Yusuf's route because she knows his habits.
explanation.tip: RL.6.1: choose evidence that directly supports the specific claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “I told Mama you'd walk the bakery way.”

options.label: C
options.text: “Your mother called every shop on this street.”
options.rationale: This is about the mother.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This shows excitement, not knowledge of Yusuf.

items.stem: Order these events from “The Last Bus Home.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The plot unfolds as a series of connected episodes from problem to resolution.
explanation.tip: Each episode leads to the next; look for cause and effect.

sequence: The robotics club stays late.
Yusuf watches the bus pull away.
His phone dies after a quick message.
He rehearses excuses while walking.
He finds Mariam waiting at the bakery.

items.stem: How does the second stanza contribute to the poem “Ladder”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stanza 2 links rung widths to specific years—an easy year, a hard year—developing the central metaphor.
explanation.tip: RL.6.5: ask what each stanza adds to the whole poem.

options.label: A
options.text: It describes how to build a ladder.
options.rationale: The poem is not instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains that the different rungs stand for different years in the speaker's life.

options.label: C
options.text: It changes the topic to apple trees.
options.rationale: Apples appear in stanza 3.

options.label: D
options.text: It introduces the grandfather for the first time.
options.rationale: He appears in stanza 1.

items.stem: What does the ladder represent in the poem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each rung is “a year he gave to me,” so the ladder stands for years of the speaker's life shaped by the grandfather.
explanation.tip: A symbol is an object that stands for a bigger idea.

options.label: A
options.text: the storm that destroyed the tree
options.rationale: The storm only explains where the branches came from.

options.label: B
options.text: a tool the speaker needs to fix the house
options.rationale: The ladder is used to reach the grandfather's apples.

options.label: C
options.text: the speaker's life and the grandfather's care that supports it

options.label: D
options.rationale: Fear is never mentioned.

items.stem: In “the third rung, thin and narrow,” what feeling do the words thin and narrow create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thin and narrow connote fragility, matching “the winter I was sick and weak.”
explanation.tip: Connotation = the feeling a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Joy would match words like wide and steady.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The year is described as hard, not dull.

options.label: C
options.rationale: No words suggest anger.

options.label: D
options.text: a sense of difficulty and weakness

items.stem: What is the author's central claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The introduction and conclusion both state the claim.
explanation.tip: The claim is the position the whole text argues for.

options.label: A
options.text: Schools should keep the five-day week until there is stronger evidence for a four-day week.

options.label: B
options.text: Four-day weeks save schools a lot of money.
options.rationale: The author argues the savings are small.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Salaries are mentioned only to explain costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Students need more rest on weekends.
options.rationale: This is the supporters' argument.

items.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the claim that a four-day week may hurt learning?

explanation.whyCorrect: A study comparing math growth is direct evidence about learning.
explanation.tip: Relevant evidence must connect directly to the specific claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Families must find care for the fifth day.
options.rationale: This is about families, not learning.

options.label: B
options.text: Math scores grew more slowly in districts that switched to four days.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the opposing view.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is about cost, not learning.

items.stem: Which claim in the text is NOT supported by reasons or evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Everyone knows” is a sweeping generalization with no evidence; it weakens the argument.
explanation.tip: RI.6.8: distinguish supported claims from unsupported ones. Watch for “everyone,” “always,” and “never.”

options.label: A
options.text: Savings are usually small because salaries do not change.
options.rationale: The author explains why with a reason.

options.label: B
options.text: Districts do save some money on buses and heating.
options.rationale: This is supported by reports.

options.label: C
options.text: Everyone knows that students would rather stay home anyway, so a four-day week would only make them lazier.

options.label: D
options.text: Students' math scores grew more slowly.
options.rationale: This is supported by a study.

items.stem: How does the author treat the claim that a four-day week saves money?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a concession and rebuttal: “Districts do save some money … but … these savings are usually small.”
explanation.tip: Strong arguments acknowledge the other side, then respond with evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: The author agrees it is the strongest reason.
options.rationale: The author argues the savings are small.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Paragraph 3 addresses it.

options.label: C
options.text: The author says it costs more money.
options.rationale: The author says districts do save some.

options.label: D
options.text: The author admits there are some savings, then shows they are small.

items.stem: True or false: The author's concluding paragraph restates the claim.

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence repeats that schools should keep the five-day schedule.
explanation.tip: Conclusions in arguments usually restate the claim.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text explains why reefs matter, the threat of bleaching, and scientists' responses.
explanation.tip: RI.6.2: the central idea is developed across the whole text.

options.label: A
options.text: Coral reefs are vital to ocean life but are threatened by warming water, and scientists are working to protect them.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a detail about the partnership.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is one example of reef life.

items.stem: Which is the best summary of paragraph 3?

explanation.whyCorrect: A good summary keeps only the key ideas of the paragraph, without opinions.
explanation.tip: Summaries are short, objective, and include only the most important points.

options.label: A
options.rationale: White coral is bleached and starving.

options.label: B
options.text: Warm water causes coral to expel its algae and turn white; if the heat lasts, the coral can die.

options.label: C
options.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines from storms.
options.rationale: That is paragraph 1.

options.label: D
options.rationale: That is paragraph 4.

items.stem: According to the text, what causes coral bleaching?

explanation.whyCorrect: “When ocean water becomes too warm … stressed corals expel their algae.”
explanation.tip: Look for “when” and “as a result” to find causes.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The algae produce the food.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Reefs break waves; this does not cause bleaching.

options.label: C
options.text: Water that is too warm makes corals expel their algae.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

items.stem: How does paragraph 2 contribute to the development of ideas in the text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Without knowing the algae feed the coral, readers wouldn't see why losing them means starving.
explanation.tip: RI.6.5: analyze how a paragraph fits into the overall structure.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Solutions come in paragraph 4.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists animals that live on reefs.
options.rationale: That is paragraph 1.

options.label: C
options.text: It argues that reefs cannot be saved.
options.rationale: The text describes hopeful efforts.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains the coral–algae partnership so readers understand why bleaching is harmful.

items.stem: Bleached coral is “not dead, but it is starving.” What does expel mean in “stressed corals expel their algae”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the algae leave and the coral turns white and starves, expel must mean force out.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.a: use the overall meaning of the paragraph as a clue.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Protection would keep the algae inside.

options.label: C
options.rationale: If the algae were fed, the coral would not starve.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Growing would not lead to bleaching.

items.stem: What is the author's point of view about efforts to save reefs?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence balances hope (“these efforts help”) with a limit (“only … if ocean temperatures stop rising”).
explanation.tip: RI.6.6: words like but and only signal the author's view.

options.label: A
options.text: The efforts are useless and should stop.
options.rationale: The author says they help.

options.label: B
options.text: The efforts are helpful, but reefs need ocean temperatures to stop rising to fully recover.

options.label: C
options.text: The efforts have already saved all reefs.
options.rationale: The author says large-scale recovery depends on temperature.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Two efforts are described.

items.stem: The Latin root aud means hear. Which word means “able to be heard”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Aud (hear) + -ible (able to be) = audible.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.b: Greek or Latin affixes and roots are clues to meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: An auditorium is a place for hearing.

options.label: B
options.rationale: An audition is a hearing for a performance.

options.label: D
options.rationale: An audience is a group that listens.

items.stem: Bio means life and logy means study of. What does a biologist study?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bio (life) + logy (study) + -ist (person) = a person who studies life.
explanation.tip: Split the word into parts and translate each one.

options.label: A
options.rationale: That is history.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is geology.

options.label: C
options.rationale: That is astronomy.

items.stem: Match each word to its meaning using roots.

explanation.whyCorrect: chron = time, bene = good, trans = across + port = carry, auto = self + graph = write.
explanation.tip: Roots appear in many related words: chronic, beneficial, portable, automatic.

items.stem: Which part of a dictionary entry tells you how to say a word?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dictionaries show pronunciation with special symbols and stress marks.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.c: consult reference materials for pronunciation and meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: the pronunciation in parentheses or slashes

options.label: B
options.rationale: Examples show usage.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Guide words help you find the page.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Definitions give meaning.

items.stem: The guide words on a dictionary page are cobalt and coconut. Which word would be on that page?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cockpit (co-c-k) comes after cobalt (co-b) and before coconut (co-c-o).
explanation.tip: Compare letter by letter until the words differ.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Coffee (co-f) comes after coconut (co-c).

options.label: C
options.rationale: Cozy (co-z) comes after coconut.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Coast (co-a) comes before cobalt (co-b).

items.stem: “The wind whispered secrets through the trees.” What figure of speech is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Whispering secrets is a human action given to the wind.
explanation.tip: L.6.5.a: interpret figures of speech in context.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration.

options.label: B
options.rationale: No like or as.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The sentence doesn't repeat beginning sounds as its main effect.

items.stem: “I've told you a million times to close the door!” What does this hyperbole mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperbole exaggerates for emphasis.
explanation.tip: Ask: is this exaggeration meant to show a feeling?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The tone is frustrated.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The sentence is about repeated reminders.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker counted exactly a million reminders.
options.rationale: Hyperbole is not meant literally.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker has said it many times and is frustrated.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A page is one part of a whole book.
explanation.tip: L.6.5.b: relationships include cause/effect, part/whole, item/category.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is cause and effect.

options.label: C
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is item and category.

items.stem: Match each word pair to its relationship.

explanation.whyCorrect: Identifying the relationship helps you understand both words.
explanation.tip: Make a sentence: “A spark CAUSES a fire,” “A wheel is PART OF a bicycle.”

items.stem: Which word has the most POSITIVE connotation for describing someone who saves money?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thrifty suggests wisely careful with money.
explanation.tip: Words with similar denotations can feel very different.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Cheap suggests being unwilling to spend, a negative feeling.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Greedy is negative and means wanting too much.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Stingy is negative.

items.stem: Which sentence makes the speaker sound most critical of the plan?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scheme connotes a sneaky or dishonest plan.
explanation.tip: Check how each word makes you feel, not just what it means.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee's plan was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Plan is neutral.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee's proposal was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Proposal is neutral or positive.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee's scheme was announced on Monday.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee's strategy was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Strategy sounds thoughtful.

items.stem: “Don't put all your eggs in one basket” advises you to —

explanation.whyCorrect: If the one basket falls, everything is lost.
explanation.tip: Proverbs give general advice about life.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The saying isn't about baskets.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The saying gives advice about risk.

options.label: D
options.text: spread your risks instead of depending on one thing

items.stem: In which sentence does object mean “to disagree”?

explanation.whyCorrect: OBject (noun) = thing or goal; obJECT (verb) = to disagree.
explanation.tip: Homographs can change meaning AND stress.

options.label: A
options.text: I object to the new rule about phones.

options.label: B
options.text: The object of the game is to score.
options.rationale: Here object means goal.

options.label: C
options.text: That shiny object is a coin.
options.rationale: Here object is a thing.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the object on the table.
options.rationale: Here object is a thing.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: “The coach gave the trophy to Laila and ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: To is a preposition, so its object must be in the objective case: me.
explanation.tip: L.6.1.a: subjective (I, he), objective (me, him), possessive (my, his).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive; there is no I in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Mine is possessive.

options.label: D
options.rationale: After a preposition (to), use the objective case.

items.stem: Which sentence uses pronoun case correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both pronouns are subjects, so both must be subjective: she and I.
explanation.tip: Test each pronoun alone: “She presented.” “I presented.”

options.label: A
options.text: She and me presented the science project.
options.rationale: Me cannot be a subject.

options.label: B
options.text: Me and her presented the science project.
options.rationale: Me and her are objective.

options.label: C
options.text: She and I presented the science project.

options.label: D
options.text: Her and me presented the science project.
options.rationale: Subjects need subjective pronouns.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an INTENSIVE pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: An intensive pronoun emphasizes a noun and could be removed without changing the meaning.
explanation.tip: Remove the -self word: if the sentence still works, it's intensive.

options.label: A
options.text: The principal handed out the awards.
options.rationale: There is no -self pronoun.

options.label: B
options.rationale: She is a subject pronoun.

options.label: C
options.text: The principal handed herself an award.
options.rationale: Here herself is reflexive (the object).

options.label: D
options.text: The principal herself handed out the awards.

items.stem: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence shifts from students (third person) to you (second person).
explanation.tip: L.6.1.c: keep pronoun number and person consistent.

options.label: A
options.text: When students study hard, you get better grades.

options.label: B
options.text: When I study hard, I get better grades.
options.rationale: Both are first person.

options.label: C
options.text: When you study hard, you get better grades.
options.rationale: Both are second person.

options.label: D
options.text: When students study hard, they get better grades.
options.rationale: Students and they are both third person.

items.stem: Which sentence has a VAGUE pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: He could mean Omar or Sami, so the reader can't tell who won.
explanation.tip: L.6.1.d: fix pronouns that could refer to more than one noun.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar told Sami that Sami had won the contest.
options.rationale: The noun is repeated, so it is clear.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar told Sami that he had won the contest.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar told Sami that Omar had won.
options.rationale: The noun makes it clear.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar told Sami, “You won the contest!”
options.rationale: The quotation makes it clear.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “It” has no clear antecedent—proud of what? Replace it with a specific noun.
explanation.tip: If you can't point to the exact noun a pronoun replaces, rewrite it.

segments: The teacher spoke to the students,
items.correction: were very proud of the results

items.stem: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Past perfect (had ended) shows the earlier of two past actions.
explanation.tip: Had + past participle = past perfect.

options.label: A
options.text: The game will have ended before we reached it.
options.rationale: Will have is future perfect.

options.label: B
options.text: The game ended before we had reach the stadium.
options.rationale: Reach should be reached.

options.label: C
options.text: The game had ended before we reached the stadium.

options.label: D
options.text: The game has ended before we reached the stadium.
options.rationale: Has ended is present perfect.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: After had, use the past participle: write → wrote → written.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs have special past participles: go/gone, eat/eaten, write/written.

items.stem: Which is a run-on sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses run together without punctuation.
explanation.tip: Fix with a period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: The library closes at six, so we need to hurry.
options.rationale: A comma and so join the clauses correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: The library closes at six; we need to hurry.
options.rationale: A semicolon joins two clauses correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the library closes at six.
options.rationale: This is a fragment, not a run-on.

options.label: D
options.text: The library closes at six we need to hurry.

items.stem: Which word is a collective noun? “The team celebrated after the final whistle.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A collective noun names a group as one unit: team, class, flock.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns are usually singular: The team IS ready.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Celebrated is a verb.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Final is an adjective.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Whistle is a common noun but not collective.

items.stem: Which shows the correct plural possessive? “The ____ uniforms were washed.”

explanation.whyCorrect: For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe: players'.
explanation.tip: Singular: player's. Plural: players'.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Do not add 's after a plural ending in s.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is plural without possession.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is singular possessive.

items.stem: Which word is a demonstrative adjective? “Those shoes belong to my brother.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Those points to specific nouns (shoes); demonstratives are this, that, these, those.
explanation.tip: Demonstrative adjectives come right before a noun.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Shoes is a noun.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Belong is a verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: My is a possessive pronoun/adjective.

items.stem: Which sentence is complex?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
explanation.tip: Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when) start dependent clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: The storm knocked out power, and school was canceled.
options.rationale: This is compound.

options.label: B
options.text: Knocked out power during the storm.
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is simple.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the storm knocked out power, school was canceled.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates the nonrestrictive element?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause adds extra information, so it is set off with commas.
explanation.tip: L.6.2.a: use commas, parentheses, or dashes for nonrestrictive elements.

options.label: A
options.text: My cousin, who lives in Jeddah, is visiting next week.

options.label: B
options.text: My cousin, who lives in Jeddah is visiting next week.
options.rationale: The closing comma is missing.

options.label: C
options.text: My cousin who lives, in Jeddah, is visiting next week.
options.rationale: The commas are in the wrong places.

options.label: D
options.text: My cousin who lives in Jeddah, is visiting next week.
options.rationale: A nonrestrictive clause needs commas on both sides.

items.stem: Which sentence uses dashes correctly to set off extra information?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pairs of dashes surround the interrupting element.
explanation.tip: Dashes, like commas, come in pairs around extra information in the middle of a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The answer—which surprised everyone was zero.
options.rationale: A second dash is needed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The dash splits the subject.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The dash must come before which.

items.stem: True or false: In “Students who finish early may read quietly,” the clause who finish early should be set off with commas.

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause is restrictive—it tells WHICH students may read—so it does not take commas.
explanation.tip: If removing the clause changes the meaning, do not use commas.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: When a quotation is interrupted by a speaker tag, use commas and keep the second part lowercase.
explanation.tip: Punctuation stays inside the quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: “I'll bring the map,” said Hana, “If you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: The sentence continues, so if is lowercase.

options.label: B
options.text: “I'll bring the map, said Hana, if you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: The speaker tag must be outside the quotation marks.

options.label: C
options.text: “I'll bring the map,” said Hana, “if you bring the snacks.”

options.label: D
options.text: “I'll bring the map” said Hana, “if you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark.

items.stem: Spell the word correctly: The tour guide will ____ (accommodate) twenty visitors.

explanation.whyCorrect: Accommodate has two c's and two m's.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: it accommodates two c's and two m's.

items.stem: Which revision best varies the sentence pattern? Original: “The sun set. The sky turned orange. Birds flew home.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Combining with an introductory clause creates variety and flow.
explanation.tip: L.6.3.a: vary sentence patterns for meaning, interest, and style.

options.label: A
options.text: The sun set. The sky turned orange. The birds flew home.
options.rationale: This keeps the same short pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Sun set. Sky orange. Birds home.
options.rationale: These are fragments.

options.label: C
options.text: The sun set and the sky turned orange and birds flew home and it was evening.
options.rationale: Too many ands makes it stringy.

options.label: D
options.text: As the sun set, the sky turned orange and birds flew home.

items.stem: Which sentence keeps a consistent formal style in a research report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Formal writing uses precise, neutral language.
explanation.tip: L.6.3.b: maintain consistency in style and tone.

options.label: A
options.text: The results indicate that students who sleep eight hours perform better on tests.

options.label: B
options.text: The results show that kids who sleep a ton do way better.
options.rationale: A ton and way better are informal.

options.label: C
options.text: Sleep is awesome for tests, LOL.
options.rationale: LOL and awesome are informal.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Casual and uses a symbol.

items.stem: Which evidence is most credible to support the claim that exercise improves concentration?

explanation.whyCorrect: Research from a reliable institution is credible and relevant.
explanation.tip: W.6.1.b: use credible sources and relevant evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: My friend says running makes him smarter.
options.rationale: One opinion is not credible evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: A university study found students focused longer after 20 minutes of activity.

options.label: C
options.text: Exercise is fun for most people.
options.rationale: Fun is not evidence about concentration.

options.label: D
options.text: An ad for sneakers says exercise boosts brain power.
options.rationale: Ads are biased sources.

items.stem: Which transition best introduces a counterclaim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Counterclaims present the other side before you respond to it.
explanation.tip: W.6.1.c: use words and phrases to clarify relationships among claims and reasons.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This introduces a first reason.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This ends an essay.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This introduces evidence, not an opposing view.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: “Coral reefs protect coastlines. ____, they provide homes for thousands of species.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Furthermore adds another important idea.
explanation.tip: W.6.2.c: use transitions to clarify relationships among ideas.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The second idea is not a result of the first.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This shows contrast.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The second sentence isn't an example of the first.

items.stem: Which source would be most reliable for a report on coral bleaching?

explanation.whyCorrect: Research institutes have experts and publish evidence.
explanation.tip: W.6.8: assess the credibility of each source.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Fiction is not factual evidence.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Anonymous sources cannot be checked.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Advertisements have a commercial purpose.

items.stem: Order the sentences to signal shifts in time and setting in a narrative.

explanation.whyCorrect: Transitions (That morning, By noon, Meanwhile, Hours later) signal shifts in time and place.
explanation.tip: W.6.3.c: use transitions to convey sequence and signal shifts.

sequence: That morning, the harbor was calm and gray.
By noon, dark clouds had gathered over the water.
Meanwhile, on the hill above town, my grandmother watched the sky.
Hours later, the storm finally passed.

items.stem: Which word is a noun? “The bird sang loudly.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A noun names a person, place, thing, or animal. Bird names an animal.
explanation.tip: Ask: can I put “a” or “the” in front of it?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Loudly is an adverb that tells how.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Sang is a verb—an action.

items.stem: Which end mark belongs at the end of this question? “Where is my pencil”

explanation.whyCorrect: Questions end with a question mark.
explanation.tip: Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why, or how.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A comma never ends a sentence.

options.label: C
options.rationale: An exclamation point shows strong feeling.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A period ends a statement, not a question.

items.stem: Which name needs a capital letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Egypt is the name of a specific place, so it is a proper noun.
explanation.tip: Specific names of people and places get capital letters.

options.label: A
options.rationale: River is a common noun.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Country is a common noun.

options.label: D
options.rationale: City is a common noun.

items.stem: Which word means the opposite of hot?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hot and cold are antonyms.
explanation.tip: Antonyms are opposites: up/down, fast/slow.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Sunny describes weather, not the opposite of hot.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Big is about size.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Warm is close to hot.

items.stem: What is the plural of box?

explanation.whyCorrect: Nouns ending in s, x, z, ch, or sh add -es.
explanation.tip: If you hear an extra syllable (box-es), add -es.

options.label: B
options.rationale: There is no y to change.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Box stays singular.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Words ending in x add -es.

items.stem: Read: “Grandpa's laugh was thunder rolling across the hills, and the children ran toward it like flowers turning to the sun.” Which statement best explains how the two comparisons work together?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thunder suggests a loud, booming laugh, while flowers turning to the sun suggests the children love being near it.
explanation.tip: With two comparisons, explain what EACH one describes, then how they connect.

options.label: A
options.text: Both comparisons describe the weather that day.
options.rationale: Thunder and sun are figurative, not real weather.

options.label: B
options.text: The metaphor shows Grandpa's laugh is big and powerful; the simile shows the children are drawn to its warmth.

options.label: C
options.text: Both comparisons show that the children are afraid of Grandpa.
options.rationale: Flowers turning to the sun shows attraction, not fear.

options.label: D
options.text: The simile describes the laugh and the metaphor describes the hills.
options.rationale: The metaphor describes the laugh; the simile describes the children.

items.stem: An article claims: “Our town should build bike lanes.” Which reason would be the WEAKEST support?

explanation.whyCorrect: The color of bikes has nothing to do with whether lanes should be built.
explanation.tip: Weak reasons are true but unrelated to the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: A nearby town's bike lanes cut pollution by 10%.
options.rationale: This is evidence from a similar place.

options.label: B
options.text: More people would bike to work, reducing traffic.
options.rationale: This explains a benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: Bikes come in many bright colors.

options.label: D
options.text: Bike lanes reduce accidents between cars and cyclists.
options.rationale: This is relevant safety evidence.

items.stem: Read: “Mira's explanation was so lucid that even her little brother understood the science experiment on the first try.” What does lucid mean, and which clue shows it?

explanation.whyCorrect: If a young child understood right away, the explanation must have been very clear.
explanation.tip: Use the RESULT described in the sentence as your clue.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Nothing suggests humor.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The brother understood, so it was not confusing.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Explanation does not tell the meaning of lucid.

options.label: D
options.text: clear — “even her little brother understood … on the first try”

items.stem: A boy brags that he will win the race, skips practice, and loses to a quieter classmate who trained every day. Which theme fits best?

explanation.whyCorrect: The events show that effort, not boasting, leads to success.
explanation.tip: Themes come from what happens to characters because of their choices.

options.label: A
options.text: Hard work matters more than bragging.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The quiet classmate wins.

options.label: C
options.text: Races are unfair to fast runners.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the race was unfair.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a lesson shown by the events.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each is singular, so the verb must be has, even though puppies is plural.
explanation.tip: Words like each, every, and either are singular subjects.

items.stem: Which word is a proper noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: Jeddah names a specific city, so it is proper and capitalized.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns name specific people, places, or things.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Market is a common noun.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Beach is a common noun.

options.label: D
options.rationale: City is a common noun.

items.stem: Which word is the verb in this sentence? “The happy children laughed.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Laughed tells what the children did.
explanation.tip: Verbs show action or being.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Children is a noun.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Happy is an adjective describing the children.

items.stem: Which sentence needs commas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Three items in a series need commas: lions, tigers, and bears.
explanation.tip: Count the items. Three or more? Use commas.

options.label: A
options.rationale: One item needs no comma.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a short simple sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: We saw lions tigers and bears.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Two items joined by and need no comma.

items.stem: What does unhappy mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The prefix un- means not.
explanation.tip: Cover the prefix, read the base word, then add the prefix meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Again is re-.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Before is pre-.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Un- does not mean very.

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Friend is spelled f-r-i-e-n-d.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: a friend to the end.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Missing the e.

options.label: C
options.rationale: i before e in friend.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Missing the i.

items.stem: A story about a soccer final is told by the goalkeeper who let in the winning goal. How would the description of the final minute most likely change if the scorer narrated it?

explanation.whyCorrect: A narrator's point of view shapes which feelings and details are emphasized.
explanation.tip: RL.5.6: ask how the narrator's experience colors the events.

options.label: A
options.text: It would describe the goalkeeper's thoughts in detail.
options.rationale: The scorer cannot know the goalkeeper's thoughts.

options.label: B
options.text: It would focus on excitement and pride instead of disappointment.

options.label: C
options.text: It would include no feelings at all.
options.rationale: First-person narrators share feelings.

options.label: D
options.text: It would describe exactly the same feelings.
options.rationale: Different narrators experience events differently.

items.stem: A text explains that honeybees pollinate crops, that bee numbers are falling, and that farmers are planting wildflower strips to help. Which statement best captures BOTH main ideas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grade 5 texts can have two main ideas: why bees matter, and how people help them.
explanation.tip: Check that your summary statement covers every section.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Honey is not discussed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a minor detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees are essential to farming, and people are acting to reverse their decline.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This misses the bees' decline and the response.

items.stem: “The early bird catches the worm.” Which situation shows this proverb?

explanation.whyCorrect: The proverb means people who act early get the best opportunities.
explanation.tip: Match the proverb's lesson to a real-life example.

options.label: A
options.text: A bird ate a worm in the garden.
options.rationale: This is the literal meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar slept late and missed the bus.
options.rationale: This shows the opposite outcome, not the proverb.

options.label: C
options.text: Lina likes birds more than worms.
options.rationale: This has nothing to do with the advice.

options.label: D
options.text: Noura arrived first at the book sale and found the rarest book.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using a dependent clause? “It was raining. We played inside.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Because it was raining is a dependent clause that explains why.
explanation.tip: Put the cause in the because-clause.

options.label: A
options.text: Because it was raining, we played inside.

options.label: B
options.text: It was raining because we played inside.
options.rationale: This reverses the cause and effect.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: D
options.text: It was raining, we played inside.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Their shows ownership (the students' notebooks); there tells where.
explanation.tip: their = belongs to them; there = place; they're = they are.

items.stem: Which word is a common noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: Teacher names a general person, not a specific one.
explanation.tip: Common nouns are not capitalized unless they start a sentence.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a specific city.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a specific name—a proper noun.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Days of the week are proper nouns.

items.stem: What kind of sentence is this? “Please close the window.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Imperative sentences give commands or requests.
explanation.tip: Declarative . | Interrogative ? | Exclamatory ! | Imperative (command).

options.label: A
options.rationale: It tells someone to do something.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It doesn't end with !

options.label: D
options.rationale: There is no question mark.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for begin?

explanation.whyCorrect: Begin and start mean the same thing.
explanation.tip: Swap the words in a sentence: if the meaning stays, they're synonyms.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Pause means stop for a while.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Finish is an antonym.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Forget is unrelated.

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “A tall building shone brightly.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Tall describes what kind of building.
explanation.tip: Adjectives answer: what kind? which one? how many?

options.label: B
options.rationale: Building is a noun.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Shone is a verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Brightly is an adverb; it tells how the building shone.

items.stem: Which word is more formal than kids?

explanation.whyCorrect: Children is the formal, standard word.
explanation.tip: Use formal words in reports and essays.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Folks is casual.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Guys is informal.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Buddies is informal.

items.stem: Which claim would require the strongest evidence to be convincing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Absolute claims (“no effect,” “any grade”) need broad, strong evidence because one counterexample can disprove them.
explanation.tip: The bigger the claim, the stronger the evidence it needs.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is an easily checked fact.

options.label: B
options.text: Some students prefer homework on weekends.
options.rationale: This is a modest claim about preference.

options.label: C
options.text: Homework has no effect on student learning at any grade level.

options.label: D
options.text: Homework can help students practise skills.
options.rationale: This is limited and widely supported.

items.stem: In a story, a girl lies to protect her friend; the lie grows, the friendship nearly breaks, and she finally confesses. The friend forgives her. Which theme is developed MOST fully?

explanation.whyCorrect: The plot moves from a lie, to consequences, to a confession that restores trust.
explanation.tip: RL.6.2: track how the theme develops through particular details.

options.label: A
options.text: Protecting friends is more important than anything.
options.rationale: The story shows the lie backfired.

options.label: B
options.text: Friends should never forgive each other.
options.rationale: The friend does forgive her.

options.label: C
options.text: Lying always works out in the end.
options.rationale: The lie nearly ruins the friendship.

options.label: D
options.text: Honesty, even when difficult, is necessary for trust between friends.

items.stem: A writer wants readers to admire a character who rarely gives up. Which word should the writer choose?

explanation.whyCorrect: Determined has a positive connotation for not giving up.
explanation.tip: Choose words whose feeling matches your purpose.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Inflexible suggests a weakness.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Stubborn suggests unreasonable refusal—a negative connotation.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Pigheaded is insulting.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Between is a preposition, so it takes the objective case: between you and me.
explanation.tip: After prepositions (between, for, with, to), use me, him, her, us, them.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to set off nonessential information?

explanation.whyCorrect: Parentheses go around extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence without the parentheses—it should still make sense.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum open (since 1985) attracts, thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The comma and parentheses are misplaced.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum (open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum (open since 1985 attracts) thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The parentheses enclose part of the main sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The (museum open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The subject is inside the parentheses.
